g9-mathematics-um6-t1.overview: Polygons are the name-and-angle grammar of flat shapes — from triangles to dodecagons. Two formulas (angle sums) plus one idea (convexity) let you measure any polygon on paper.
objectives: Name polygons by side-count and classify convex vs concave
Derive and use the interior angle-sum formula (n−2)·180°
Find each interior/exterior angle of a regular polygon
g9-mathematics-um6-t1.simple: A polygon is a closed shape of straight sides: 3 = triangle, 4 = quadrilateral, 5 = pentagon, 6 = hexagon… Any n-gon splits into (n−2) triangles from one vertex, so its interior angles total (n−2)×180°: pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°. Walk around ANY convex polygon and you turn exactly one full circle — exterior angles always sum to 360°. For a REGULAR polygon (all sides and angles equal), just divide: each interior angle = (n−2)·180/n.
g9-mathematics-um6-t1.detailed:
Polygon vocabulary: sides and vertices (corners); a diagonal joins non-adjacent vertices — an n-gon has n(n−3)/2 of them (each of n vertices reaches n−3 others, halved for double-counting). Convex: every interior angle < 180° and all diagonals lie inside; concave has at least one reflex angle. A regular polygon is both equilateral and equiangular.

The interior sum S = (n − 2)·180° comes from triangulation: from one vertex, draw diagonals to all non-neighbours, splitting the n-gon into exactly n − 2 triangles. A quadrilateral gives 360°, confirming the rectangle fact. Rearranged for regular polygons: each interior angle = (n−2)·180°/n — for a hexagon, 720/6 = 120°.

At every vertex, interior + exterior = 180° (straight line). Going once around a convex polygon, the exterior (turning) angles sum to 360° — independent of n, because you complete one full rotation. Hence each exterior angle of a regular n-gon is 360°/n, and interior = 180° − 360°/n — the same formula, cleaner route. This also solves 'for what n is the interior angle 175°?': exterior 5° → n = 360/5 = 72.

Angle chasing mixes the tools: an unknown exterior from a given interior (subtract from 180), an n recovered from an interior angle (via exterior 360/n), or a missing angle in an irregular polygon (total minus the rest). Watch the classic exam inversion: 'interior angle is 3 times the exterior' → x + 3x = 180 → exterior 45° → n = 8.

Proof culture: the formulas are theorem-statements worth re-deriving in one line (triangulation; one full turn). Knowing WHY prevents the (n+2) misremembering and lets you recover constants under exam stress.

g9-mathematics-um6-t1.summary: Convex n-gons hold (n−2)·180° of interior angles and 360° of exterior ones. Regular polygons divide both evenly: interior = 180 − 360/n, and n follows from 360/exterior. Diagonals: n(n−3)/2. Angle chasing alternates the sum, the supplement, and the constant 360°.

g9-mathematics-um6-t2.overview: Tessellations are polygons packed with no gaps and no overlaps — a puzzle with a strict admission rule: the angles meeting at every vertex must total exactly 360°.
objectives: Define tessellation and distinguish regular from semi-regular
Test which regular polygons tessellate alone
Verify vertex configurations with angle sums
Explain why only 3 regular shapes tile the plane
g9-mathematics-um6-t2.simple: Tile a bathroom floor with identical regular shapes, edge to edge, no gaps: squares work (4 × 90° = 360°), hexagons work (3 × 120° = 360°), triangles work (6 × 60° = 360°). Pentagons fail — 108° never divides 360 evenly (3 × 108 = 324, leaves a 36° hole). That vertex rule — angles around every junction = 360° exactly — decides every tessellation, single or mixed.
g9-mathematics-um6-t2.detailed:
A tessellation covers the plane with copies of a shape, edge-to-edge, no gaps or overlaps. A regular tessellation uses one kind of regular polygon; its vertex type is written by the polygon counts around a point, e.g. squares = 4.4.4.4 (or 4⁴). The divisibility test: regular n-gon interior angle (180 − 360/n) must divide 360 evenly — check k·(180−360/n) = 360 for integer k ≥ 3. Only n = 3 (k=6), 4 (k=4), 6 (k=3) survive: hence exactly THREE regular tessellations.

Why so few? As n grows the interior angle passes 120° toward 180°, and you can never fit three around a point beyond the hexagon; below that, the pentagon's 108° straddles 360 without landing on it. The vertex rule is the master: at every junction, angle-sum = 360° — verify candidates by arithmetic, reject by leftover gap or overlap.

Semi-regular (Archimedean) tessellations mix ≥2 regular polygons with the SAME vertex configuration everywhere — 8 families exist, e.g. 3.3.3.4.4 (two triangles then two squares... precisely triangle-triangle-triangle-square-square): 60×3 + 90×2 = 360 ✓; and 3.3.3.3.6 (four triangles + hexagon): 240 + 120 = 360 ✓. Uniformity across all vertices is what makes them 'Archimedean'; random legal mixes that vary vertex-to-vertex are merely 'demiregular'.

Hands-on verification mirrors the math: cut paper hexagons and watch three meet perfectly at a point; try pentagons and see the 36° gap. Conversely, any triangle or quadrilateral tessellates — rotate a copy 180° about a side midpoint to complete a parallelogram-ish strip; the curved 'Escher' style keeps the edge-complement trick. Irregular tiling escapes the vertex rule because its angles pair out instead.

Real culture: the Alhambra's walls prefigure all 17 wallpaper symmetry groups; Islamic girih patterns ride on 6⁴ and 3.3.3.3.3.3 lattices; crystallography sees 6-fold rings in benzene and snow quasicrystals. For exams, the two standard tasks are 'does this shape tessellate?' (do the angle division) and 'complete the vertex 3.12.12?' (60 + 150 + 150 = 360 ✓ — triangle and two dodecagons).

Mixes yield the 8 Archimedean types — verify each by adding interior angles. Non-regular triangles/quadrilaterals always tile by 180° rotation tricks.
